extracted.intended_audience: humor researchers, pragmatics/linguistics scholars, joke analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Taxonomy and analytic procedure for classifying jokes by (a) the source of incongruity (frame-based vs discourse-centered), (b) where it occurs (setup vs punchline), and (c) the type of resolution (frame-, discourse-, or implication-based). Includes corpus methods and inferential sub-strategies for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case 5: frame-based incongruity (setup) — implication-based resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jokes instantiate a frame-based incongruity located in the setup; the hearer constructs an adequate make-sense frame for the setup and must derive implicatures beyond the explicit interpretation to resolve the incongruity. This Case is not very frequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolution is mainly carried out through derivation of implicated premises and conclusions beyond the inferred explicit interpretation. Analysts should look for an initially plausible frame in the setup that leads to implicatures later (example (18) where a funeral frame yields an unexpected motive to buy a mule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case 6: frame-based incongruity (punchline) — implication-based resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The source of incongruity is located in the punchline; the hearer must derive a number of implications (strong and weak implicatures) after the punchline alters the previously constructed frame. This Case is rather frequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should track how the punchline forces the hearer to alter the initial frame and to construct several implicated premises/conclusions (example (19) leading to implications (20a–e)). Consider both speaker-intended implicatures and hearer-generated weak implicatures; relate to Curcó's key/target assumption distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case 7: discourse-centered incongruity (setup) — discourse-based resolution (garden-path)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical joke structure in which an element in the setup has covert ambiguity with one effortlessly accessible meaning; the punchline invalidates the earlier inference, prompting backtracking and reprocessing of the setup (garden-path mechanism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for initial covert ambiguity in the setup and a punchline that foregrounds an alternative interpretation, forcing inferential backtracking. Examples: syntactic/structural reanalysis (22), unarticulated constituents (23), referent reassignment (24), sense ambiguity (25), reinterpretation of a concept's expected connotation (26).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case 8: discourse-centered incongruity (punchline) — discourse-based resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Source of discourse-centered incongruity is in the punchline; the punchline ends in an ambiguity where both interpretations are entertained simultaneously, and resolution depends on co-entertainment rather than replacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify final-word polysemy or punchline ambiguity that leaves both senses active (example (27) 'You get repossessed!' plays with repossess/repossessed meanings). Resolution relies on equal accessibility of both interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case 9: discourse-centered incongruity (setup) — frame-based resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Source of incongruity is in the setup (discourse-centered) but the resolution requires a variation of the make-sense frame constructed so far (change of scenario). This Case is less frequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect ambiguous setup elements whose reinterpretation forces a frame change (example (28) 'while you're making love' shifting from married sex to sex with a lover). Also note potential additional implicatures about characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case 10: discourse-centered incongruity (punchline) — frame-based resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Rare pattern where the punchline contains the incongruity and resolving it requires adjusting a concept (e.g., 'idiots') and then reconstructing the frame to fit the altered quality of a character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for punchlines that require concept adjustment and consequent reconstruction of the overall frame (example (29) physics professor keeps 'idiots' out of medical school).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case 11: discourse-centered incongruity (setup) — implication-based resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Discourse-centered incongruity in the setup that demands derivation of several implications to resolve the mismatch; often based on concept adjustment in the setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify setup ambiguities/metaphors that require concept adjustment and the derivation of implicated premises about social situations (examples (30) and (31) adjusting 'sacrifice' and 'dead body').

rubrics_metrics.name: Case 12: discourse-centered incongruity (punchline) — implication-based resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Discourse-centered incongruity in the punchline where the hearer must adjust coded concepts in the punchline and then derive implicatures (often about characters' sexuality or personality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track how punchline-coded concepts are broadened/metaphorically applied (examples (32) 'trying to get my date drunk' used to mean the man's hand; (33) 'find a suitable stone' metaphorically for heart). Analysts should look for derivation of both strong and weak implicatures from these adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy axes: source/location/resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes are classified along three binary/ternary axes: source of incongruity (frame-based vs discourse-centered), location of source (setup vs punchline), and type of resolution required (discourse-based, frame-based, or implication-based).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ascription to a Case requires identifying (1) source type, (2) whether the incongruity element is in the setup or punchline, and (3) which resolution strategy (discourse, frame, or implicature derivation) reconciles the incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferential sub-strategies for discourse-centered incongruities
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of sub-strategies analysts must consider when analyzing discourse-centered incongruities: identification of logical form, retrieval of unarticulated constituents, reference assignment, disambiguation, and concept adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sub-analysis for Cases 7–12 should record which sub-strategy(ies) are at work; ambiguous jokes may involve multiple candidate sub-strategies (example (35) where 'bring' could be polysemy, ad hoc concept formation, or a general sense narrowed in context). Table 4 summarizes observed frequencies per sub-strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for ascribing jokes to Cases (inferential tracking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three-step analytic procedure: (1) spot source of incongruity (frame-based or discourse-centered), (2) check where the incongruity is located (setup or punchline), (3) focus on kind of resolution needed (discourse-, implication- or frame-based).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform 'inferential tracking' neutrally (analyst dissecting the joke). Be aware that jokes told in context may yield interpretive variation due to audience background; note problematic ascription cases where multiple strategies apply or classification is uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corpus collection and sampling criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpus of 500 jokes randomly selected from an online repository (jokes2go.net) across multiple topical sections (marriage, sex roles, bar, travel, sex, blonde, jobs, doctor, religion, lawyer, sport, family, other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sampling, note differing sizes of sections and take random samples across sections. The paper reports counts per topic (e.g., marriage 88, sex 98, doctor 73, lawyer 64, bar 55) and uses these to analyze Case distribution by topic (Table 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency metrics and distributional measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative metrics used: counts and percentages of jokes per Case, Case-by-topic frequency (Tables 2 and 3), and inferential sub-strategy frequencies (Table 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both raw counts and percentages (e.g., frame-based jokes: 329/490 = 67.14%; discourse-centered: 161/490 = 32.86%; forward incongruities: 344/490 = 70.2%). Use these to support claims about designers' preferences and Case prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward vs backward incongruity distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Forward incongruities: inferential procedures that add to the processing of the joke (hearer constructs a new frame or derives implicatures after processing); backward incongruities: punchline forces backtracking to re-interpret the setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure prevalence (forward favored in corpus). Analysts should note that forward incongruities often increase personalization and satisfaction because the hearer finds the solution themselves; backward incongruities force reprocessing and are less common in the corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal vs cultural belief representation (stereotype-consistency criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between representations stored as personal/private beliefs ('I believe that p') and those stored as cultural/meta-representations ('in this culture it is believed that p'); this affects whether stereotype-consistent jokes produce incongruity for recipients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing stereotype-based jokes (e.g., (34) beer/female hormones), consider the hearer's personal vs cultural beliefs: if private beliefs match the stereotype, the joke may not present an incongruity. Account for metarepresentational storage in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling problematic Case ascription
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jokes resist clean classification (multiple discourse-centered sub-strategies, ambiguous source/location/resolution); these are flagged as 'problematic Case ascription' and counted separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record problematic cases (10 in corpus) and note possible multiple sub-strategies. Analysts should transparently report ambiguous ascriptions rather than force a single Case label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of strong vs weak implicatures in humor (cognitive overload)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous effects may rely on a mix of strong implicatures clearly intended by the speaker and weak implicatures recovered by hearers; a large array of weak implicatures can create 'cognitive overload' that contributes to humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish intended (strong) implicatures from hearer-generated (weak) ones. Document the range of assumptions a joke elicits (example (36) and derived assumptions (37a–f)) and consider the contribution of weak implicatures to overall humorous effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetrical incongruity-resolution pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: In discourse-centered incongruities, the most frequent pattern is symmetrical incongruity-resolution: the same inferential sub-strategy is used both as the source of incongruity and in its resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding Cases 7–12, check whether the sub-strategy that creates the incongruity (e.g., disambiguation) is the same one used in the resolution; record symmetry as an analytic feature (noted as common in the corpus).
